findings.explanation: In GISLookup.process_band_indices (new code), self.band_rhs is assigned directly from self.rhs[1] (the second element of the user-supplied lookup tuple) with no int() validation or allowlist. This value is then concatenated into raw SQL text in PostGISOperator.check_raster via `template_params['rhs'] = '%s, %s' % (template_params['rhs'], lookup.band_rhs)` rather than passed as a bound parameter. An attacker who controls the lookup tuple value (e.g. `RasterField.objects.filter(raster__exact=(raster, '1) OR 1=1 --')`) can inject arbitrary SQL. The parallel band_lhs path is safe because RasterField.get_transform enforces `int(name)`, but band_rhs has no such guard.

evidence.content: SQL injection is a type of attack where a malicious user is able to execute arbitrary SQL code on a database. This can result in records being deleted or data leakage.

findings.suggested_fix: Validate the band index before use, e.g. `self.band_rhs = int(self.rhs[1])` (raising a clear error on failure), mirroring the int() coercion already applied to band_lhs in RasterField.get_transform, so only a numeric identifier is ever interpolated into the SQL text.

findings.explanation: The new raster branch of getquoted() (adapter.py:67-69) builds the SQL literal by directly string-interpolating self.ewkb into a quoted, cast expression: `"'%s'::raster" % self.ewkb`. Unlike the geometry branch, which delegates to psycopg2's Binary adapter (properly escaped/parameterized), this raster path inlines the value into the SQL text. self.ewkb is the output of to_pgraster(obj), which hexlifies the raw raster band data (pgraster.py:155 `binascii.hexlify(band.data(...))`). If a GDALRaster's band data is ever derived from user-supplied input, any non-hex bytes (e.g. a single-quote) embedded in the hexlified string would terminate the single-quoted literal and allow arbitrary SQL injection. The project's own security policy (docs/topics/security.txt) requires that user-controllable parameters be properly escaped/parameterized, and this changed line bypasses the driver's escaping. This is a missing-authorization/escaping control on a newly added code path.

evidence.content: SQL injection is a type of attack where a malicious user is able to execute arbitrary SQL code on a database. ... you should always be careful to properly escape any parameters that the user can control.

findings.suggested_fix: Do not inline the raster value into the SQL string. Pass the raster as a bound parameter (e.g. via psycopg2 Binary or a parameterized query) so the driver escapes it, or strictly validate that self.ewkb contains only [0-9A-F] hex characters before interpolation and reject otherwise.

.. _sql-injection-protection:

SQL injection protection
========================

SQL injection is a type of attack where a malicious user is able to execute
arbitrary SQL code on a database. This can result in records
being deleted or data leakage.

By using Django's querysets, the resulting SQL will be properly escaped by
the underlying database driver. However, Django also gives developers power to
write :ref:`raw queries <executing-raw-queries>` or execute
:ref:`custom sql <executing-custom-sql>`. These capabilities should be used
sparingly and you should always be careful to properly escape any parameters
that the user can control. In addition, you should exercise caution when using
:meth:`~django.db.models.query.QuerySet.extra` and
:class:`~django.db.models.expressions.RawSQL`.

Clickjacking protection
=======================

Clickjacking is a type of attack where a malicious site wraps another site
in a frame. This attack can result in an unsuspecting user being tricked
into performing unintended actions on the target site.

Django contains :ref:`clickjacking protection <clickjacking-prevention>` in
the form of the
:mod:`X-Frame-Options middleware <django.middleware.clickjacking.XFrameOptionsMiddleware>`
which in a supporting browser can prevent a site from being rendered inside
a frame. It is possible to disable the protection on a per view basis
or to configure the exact header value sent.

The middleware is strongly recommended for any site that does not need to have
its pages wrapped in a frame by third party sites, or only needs to allow that
for a small section of the site.

Percent literals in ``cursor.execute`` queries
----------------------------------------------

When you are running raw SQL queries through the
:ref:`cursor.execute <executing-custom-sql>` method, the rule about doubling
percent literals (``%``) inside the query has been unified. Past behavior
depended on the database backend. Now, across all backends, you only need to
double literal percent characters if you are also providing replacement
parameters. For example::

    # No parameters, no percent doubling
    cursor.execute("SELECT foo FROM bar WHERE baz = '30%'")

    # Parameters passed, non-placeholders have to be doubled
    cursor.execute("SELECT foo FROM bar WHERE baz = '30%%' and id = %s", [self.id])

``SQLite`` users need to check and update such queries.
